title: Large language models, what they are and how they are trained

items.context:
Lecture 16's generative models drew a whole point (x, y) at once. How does an LLM draw a
text?
items.why:
A 10-token text already has about 10^47 possible values, far too many to draw at once.
One token at a time, each step is one choice among 50,257, and the chain rule makes the
result exact.
items.true: One token at a time, each given the tokens before it
false: Every token at once, like one sample from a Gaussian mixture
Word by word, with each word drawn independently
As one whole sentence, picked from a list of candidates

items.context: Why is a model that only predicts the next token a complete model of text?
items.why:
p(x_1, ..., x_T) = product over t of p(x_t | all earlier tokens). This is exact, with no
assumption about which earlier tokens matter. Learn the next-token probabilities and you
have the whole distribution.
items.true: The chain rule makes p(text) a product of next-token probabilities
false: Each token depends only on the token right before it
It approximates p(text), and the error shrinks as models get bigger
Texts are short, so little is lost by going one token at a time

items.context:
An LLM writing an answer works like Lecture 8's recursive AR forecast. Which weakness do
they share?
items.why:
Both use their own predictions as later inputs. In Lecture 8 the forecast was worse than
the mean after two hours; in an LLM, one wrong token early on steers the rest of the answer.
items.true: Each output is fed back in, so an early error carries forward
false: Both can only use a fixed window of the last 10 values
Both are linear models, so they cannot capture curved trends in data
Both must be trained on labels written by people

items.context: Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary by repeating one step. Which?
items.why:
Start from characters, count every adjacent pair, merge the most frequent one into a new
token, repeat. In "aaabdaaabac" the first merge is a + a, which appears 4 times.
items.true: Merge the most frequent pair of neighboring tokens
false: Split the longest token in the vocabulary into two shorter ones
Add every whole word that appears at least twice in the text
Drop the rarest characters from the vocabulary

items.context: Why do LLMs cut text into subwords rather than whole words?
items.why:
A word vocabulary has no token for a word it never saw. With subwords, common words stay
whole and rare ones split ("overhe" + "ated"), so any text can be written. Whole words give
fewer tokens, not more.
items.true: A new word, like the pump tag P-101A, can still be built from pieces
false: Attention can compare only pieces of words, never whole words at once
Whole words would make every text many more tokens long
Subwords make every word exactly two tokens, so costs are fixed

items.context: The tokenizer cuts "4140" into "414" and "0". What should you do with unit conversions?
items.why:
The model predicts digits as tokens; it does not calculate. Scientific notation splits into
even more pieces: "Q = 1.5e-3 m³/s" is 15 characters and 12 tokens.
items.true: Do them in code: the model sees text pieces, not a quantity
false: Write numbers in scientific notation so each stays one token
Raise the temperature so the model explores more digits
Nothing: the model rebuilds the number before computing

items.context:
You paste a manual longer than the model's context window. What happens to the part past
the window?
items.why:
The context window is the most tokens the model can take in at once. Text beyond it is not
part of the input, so long documents must be cut, summarized or searched first.
items.true: The model never sees it
false: It is read, but with lower attention weights
It is summarized automatically before answering
It is stored and read on your next question

items.context: An LLM uses Lecture 12's transformer with one change. Which?
items.why:
The mask sets the scores of later tokens to minus infinity, so their weights are 0. The
prediction at position t uses only tokens 1 to t, and in training the answer stays hidden.
items.true: A causal mask: each token sees only itself and earlier tokens
false: No attention at all: each token goes through the MLP on its own
Each token attends only to the single token right before it
The tokens are read from right to left, so the answer comes first

items.context: Pretraining uses trillions of tokens that nobody labeled. Where do the targets come from?
items.why:
The target at every position is the token that actually came next. That is why any text
can be used, without anyone labeling it.
items.true: The text itself, shifted by one token
false: People who label a small sample of it
A smaller model that labels it first
The tokenizer, which marks tokens right or wrong

items.context:
The pretraining loss is the cross-entropy of Lecture 10. At each position, what is being
classified?
items.why:
Each position is a classification with one class per token: 50,257 classes for GPT-2, 129
for our tiny GPT. The loss is minus the log of the probability given to the true class.
items.true: The next token, among all tokens in the vocabulary
false: Whether the sentence so far is true or false
The topic of the document the text came from
Whether the token is a whole word or a piece of one

items.context:
Our tiny GPT has 842,881 parameters, 58 ms per training step, and gradients from
backpropagation (Lecture 11). Where does it sit on Lecture 15's optimizer map?
items.why:
Lecture 15's reactor had 2 knobs and hours per experiment: Bayesian optimization. Hundreds
of thousands of parameters with cheap gradients is gradient territory; GPT-3 used Adam,
Llama 3 AdamW.
items.true: Gradient-based: many inputs, cheap steps, gradients available
false: Bayesian optimization: few inputs, expensive experiments
A grid search over every parameter, one at a time
Derivative-free search, since a noisy loss makes gradients useless

items.context:
The tiny GPT ends with a training loss of 1.22 and a held-out loss of 1.51. What does the
gap tell you?
items.why:
With 0.6 million characters, the training loss keeps falling while the held-out loss levels
off: Lecture 9's overfitting. More steps widen the gap; the held-out curve is the one to
trust.
items.true: It has started to memorize its training text: overfitting
false: It is undertrained, and more steps will close the gap
The held-out notes use characters the model never saw in training
The learning rate is too low to reach the held-out text

items.context: The held-out loss is 1.51, and e^(-1.51) is about 0.22. What does 22% mean?
items.why:
The loss is the average of -ln p, so e^(-loss) is the typical p: the geometric mean of the
probabilities given to the true characters. It is not the share of right guesses. A blind
guess gives 1/129, 0.8%.
items.true: The true next character typically gets about 22% probability
false: 22% of the model's next-character guesses are right
The model has learned 22% of its 129-character vocabulary
Training is 22% of the way from a blind guess to a loss of zero

items.context:
Trained on our notes alone, the tiny GPT finishes 15 of 16 course terms but writes no
meaningful sentence. What would help most?
items.why:
It already copies our style. Meaning takes far more data and parameters; training longer on
0.6 million characters only memorizes them, as the held-out loss shows.
items.true: Far more text, and a bigger model
false: Training longer on the same notes
A higher sampling temperature
A longer context window

items.context: DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters, 37 billion of them active. What does "active" mean?
items.why:
DeepSeek-V3 is a mixture of experts: for each token, only some of its expert sub-networks
run. All 671 billion parameters are trained; 37 billion do the work on any one token, which
keeps each step cheaper.
items.true: Only part of the parameters is used for each token
false: Only 37 billion were trained; the rest are left random
The rest are kept for languages other than English
The rest switch on only at a high temperature

items.context:
Asked a question, a pretrained model continues the text instead of answering. What turns it
into a chat model?
items.why:
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on examples of good answers; RLHF or DPO then trains on
which of two answers people prefer. More pretraining only makes it better at continuing
text.
items.true: More training on good answers, then on people's preferences
false: More pretraining on web text, until it learns to answer on its own
A larger context window, so it sees the whole question
A lower temperature, so it picks the most likely answer

items.context: You lower the temperature from 1 to 0.3. What happens to the next-token probabilities?
items.why:
The logits are divided by the temperature before the softmax. Dividing by 0.3 stretches the
gaps, so the most likely token takes more of the probability.
items.true: The top token takes more of them: safer, more repetitive text
false: They flatten, so unlikely tokens get a real chance
They stay the same; only the speed of generation changes a little
Only the most common words in the vocabulary remain

items.context:
The softmax with a temperature is Boltzmann's distribution. In that parallel, what does a
token's logit play?
items.why:
exp(z/τ) matches exp(-E/k_BT): a high logit is a low energy, and τ plays k_BT. Cold, the
lowest-energy state (the top token) wins; hot, every state gets visited.
items.true: Minus the energy of a state
false: The temperature k_BT of the system
The number of states the system can visit
The entropy of the system

items.context: Why can an LLM state a wrong number as fluently as a right one?
items.why:
Pretraining makes likely text likely, true or not. After "…100 degrees", Qwen gave
"Fahrenheit" 58.6% for water's boiling point and took it. Check every number and unit.
items.true: Its loss rewards the likely next token; nothing checks facts
false: Numbers split into tokens, and it cannot read the tokens back
A low temperature forces it to guess when unsure
It was trained on simulations, not on measurements

items.context:
The same prompt can give a different answer, even at temperature 0. As in Lecture 1, what
should you save?
items.why:
Providers do not promise identical outputs for identical inputs. A result you cannot
regenerate has to be stored, with what produced it: Lecture 1's reproducibility rule.
items.true: The output you used, with the model's name and the date
false: Only the prompt, since the same output can always be regenerated
The temperature setting, which fixes the output
Nothing: rerun the prompt whenever you need the answer
